The story contains several character and plot developments that subvert typical tropes while remaining completely consistent with the established world and characters. 

For example, when Marnie marries into a wealthy Southern family with a formidable matriarch, the expected cliché is that the mother-in-law (Miss Emily) will be outright hostile and try to drive her away. Instead, the story takes a surprising turn: Miss Emily isn't mean; she is "paying attention" and taking "inventory." This culminates in Miss Emily offering Marnie a secret consulting role in the family business. While surprising, this turn is completely appropriate in hindsight. The narrative carefully sets up Miss Emily as a pragmatic, self-made businesswoman who values competence and observation above all else, and earlier scenes establish Marnie’s unique, sharp intuition learned from eleven years behind a cash register. 

Similarly, Teddy's reaction to Marnie being given a real responsibility in the company—admitting without bitterness that his own job is a fake title his mother invented for him, and genuinely supporting Marnie—subverts the expectation of marital jealousy, yet fits perfectly with his established easygoing, self-aware, and "soft" personality.
